title: Solo founder, AI-built multiplayer pixel world in the browser, looking for feedback
author: Level_Imagination544
selftext:
I'm a solo founder and I've been building OriginForge Connect, a multiplayer pixel world in the browser where founders and builders explore, fish, mine and build their own homes. Full transparency: I designed and directed it, and it was built with heavy AI help: the code, the pixel art (drawn by scripts) and the music were all AI-generated from my briefs. Lantern Night, its free Halloween event, starts 31 October. Would love feedback from anyone who likes cosy multiplayer worlds.

**How I built it with AI**

I'm not writing the code myself. I direct the development and use Claude as my lead developer. I explain each feature in plain English, including how it should work, how it should feel and the rules it needs to follow. For example, I want to avoid paid services where possible, keep chat restricted for under-18s, and make everything free for testers.

Claude writes the code, creates pixel art using scripts and helps build the music. But that doesn't mean I just accept whatever it produces. I play every build myself and have six testers from X helping me put it through its paces. I send back screenshots, console errors and feedback when something doesn't feel right, then work through the fixes with Claude.

The world, characters and story come from me. I'm a fantasy author, so the creative direction is mine, although testers have contributed ideas too. One suggested the Headless Rider, for example.

Some of the hardest problems have been multiplayer and saving progress. I've had issues with houses not saving properly and players appearing in the wrong places. Those took several rounds of testing, investigating and fixing before we could get them behaving as intended.

For me, the process isn't just asking AI to make a game and hoping for the best. It's directing the development, making decisions, testing what gets built and working through the problems until it starts coming together.
